# T1 v2 script draft (Claude). Ingest verbatim via write_checkpoint. Do not edit text.

## scene_001: The Arrival in London

You had eight hours to live. That was the sweating sickness. I step off a ferry onto the wet stones of London on a gray evening in September, fourteen eighty-five. The tide stinks of mud and old fish. The lanes climb away between leaning timber houses, dark as the inside of a barrel. I pull my cloak tighter and walk uphill, my boots sticking in the mire. Records place the first deaths of this strange sickness in the city on the nineteenth of September, fourteen eighty-five. Nobody around me knows it yet. A baker bangs his shutters closed. It is an ordinary evening in a city about to learn a new and terrible word. I keep walking, and I listen for it.

## scene_002: The Speed of the Killer

I follow a woman's voice into a narrow yard behind a cloth merchant's house. A man sat at his table at noon, she tells a neighbor, eating bread and laughing. Now he lies upstairs shaking with fever, and the sheets are soaked through. I stand by the well and count the church bells. This is what frightens everyone. Accounts of the outbreak say the onset was sudden, and that death or recovery often came within eight to ten hours. A man could sit down to supper and be gone before morning. I look up at the window where the candle burns. Whatever is happening in that room will be decided before the sun rises.

## scene_003: The Leaders Fall

By the next morning I stand in a market lane where people speak in low voices and watch each other's faces for the first flush of fever. Over the coming weeks the sickness reaches into the finest houses of the city. Among those who died were two lord mayors of London, six aldermen, and three sheriffs. I watch a line of men in dark gowns walk behind a coffin toward a church door, and I notice how many of them glance at one another. Each knows the man beside him may be next. Rank was no shield here, and the bells rang for rich and poor.

## scene_004: The Vigil

I am let into a house where a family keeps vigil, perhaps because no one has the strength to ask who I am. The room is hot and close and smells of wet wool and tallow. A man lies on a low bed, his face flushed, his hair plastered to his forehead. Sweat runs from him in streams. His wife wrings a cloth into a basin and presses it to his neck. A boy sits on the floor with his knees drawn up, watching the candle shrink. The bell of the nearest church rings, and the wife flinches as if it were counting something. I do not know how this night will end. Neither do they.

## scene_005: Who It Struck

In the morning I walk through a churchyard where fresh earth is heaped in rows. Historians describe the sickness falling hardest on men in the middle of adult life, often among the well off. Some accounts say infants and small children were spared. Across the lane, two small children sit on a doorstep tearing a loaf of bread between them, while their father stands at the window with a hand pressed to his mouth. It is a strange sight, and nobody around me can explain it. I hear only the scrape of spades and the slow closing of doors up and down the street.

## scene_006: A City Holding Its Breath

By midweek the city has changed its pace. People walk in the middle of the lane, away from doorways, and they do not stop to talk. I see a priest hurrying past with a lantern, his lips moving in prayer. At a crossing a crowd gathers around a shouting man who says the end of the world is at hand, and some of them listen while others walk away. I stop at a tavern window and look inside. A single drinker stares into his cup as though it might speak. Nobody here knows what to blame, so they blame everything.

## scene_007: The Question Nobody Can Answer

I leave the lane, and the centuries slide from my shoulders like a dropped cloak. Now I sit in a quiet reading room with a lamp and a stack of books. Here the question is not who will die tonight, but what the killer was. The honest answer is that nobody knows. Its cause remains unknown. Some researchers have suggested a species of hantavirus. In two thousand and four, a microbiologist named Edward McSweegan suggested anthrax. Neither idea has settled the matter. I turn the pages and the same gap keeps appearing. The sickness is recorded, but never explained.

## scene_008: The Quiet at the End of October

I step back into London, and it is late October. The air has turned sharp and bright, and the lanes feel quieter, as though the whole city is holding its breath. The sickness is ending, and no one around me can say why. By the end of October it had killed several thousand people in London. I stand before a row of shuttered houses, each with one dark window, and I count them without meaning to. I think of how many people never reached this quieter week. In some houses the shutters will open again. In others they will stay closed for a long time.

## scene_009: The Man in the Doorway

On the thirtieth of October, bells ring across the city, and this time they are not tolling for the dead. Henry the Seventh is crowned king. I move with the crowd along the street, among faces that are pale and tired but alive. At the corner of a lane I stop. I know this doorway. It is the house of the vigil. The man from the low bed stands there, thin and gray, holding the frame with both hands. The boy leans against his leg. The man is breathing. His eyes follow the crowd going by. The hours that killed so many of his neighbors ended differently for him. He simply stands there, alive, listening to the bells as though hearing them for the first time.

## scene_010: A Storm That Passed

I travel forward and stand in a hall of archives, where the air is cool and still. Here scholars have set the English sweat beside the other epidemics of its age and found that it behaved differently. Other epidemics were typically urban and lingered for a long time. This one spiked and receded very quickly, and it fell heavily on rural people as well. Historians count five epidemics between fourteen eighty-five and fifteen fifty-one. Each account records a season of fear, and each season ended almost as suddenly as it began. It reads like a storm passing over a country, loud and violent, then gone.

## scene_011: The Last Autumn

I walk on to fifteen fifty-one. The last outbreak is under way, and the lanes are tense and quiet again. After that year the disease apparently vanished from the record. I look for a sign of what ended it, and the streets give me none. There are only the ordinary sounds of a city going back to its work. I stand in the middle of the lane and wait for the sickness to return, and it does not. The English sweat arrived in September of fourteen eighty-five, took its thousands, and left without ever explaining itself.

## scene_012: The Bridge

I leave the past behind me, and I am standing on a stone bridge in the present day. The same river runs beneath me, wide and dark, carrying the lights of the city on its back. The wind is cold against my face. I think of the man in his doorway, and of the boy beside him. Mist is rising from the water. A single lantern burns at the end of the bridge. Then a lone barge slides out from beneath the arches and drifts downstream into the dark. I watch it until the mist takes it.
